name: The L & H Route (Free Variation)
approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns (and a similar distance from the Washington Pass summit). From the highway, head directly uphill toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
descent: Rappel the Ellen Pea route with two ropes, or walk off to the west

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: This is the honest answer for most objectives here: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

name: North Ridge
approach: From the Alpental lot, hike the Snow Lake Trail to the signed split onto the Source Lake Overlook trail, and take it. Past Source Lake the path crosses talus, then a cairned climbers' path leaves left and skirts beneath the cliffs into the basin below Bryant, Hemlock and The Tooth, with Pineapple Pass (about 5,280 ft) at the head of the basin. The North Ridge starts on the north side of the peak: from the basin drop about 100 ft and traverse northwest to reach the ridge crest.

name: The West Face
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft), follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, pass South Early Winters Spire, and traverse left along the base to the shared start with the Northwest Corner. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base.
descent: Two options: the original descent goes down and skier's-left of the summit via three single-rope rappels to the notch, then one free-hanging rappel past the chockstone, then a scramble out; a newer line uses six bolted rappel stations, starting about 15 ft climber's-right of the route's top.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, first come first served

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee
bivy.capacity: First come first served

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park
bivy.capacity: Scattered dispersed sites, small parties

name: Thunder Mountain North Face
approach: Reached via the same Trap Pass approach used for Slippery Slab Tower (Tunnel Creek or Surprise Creek trailheads to the PCT at Trap Pass), continuing past Slippery Slab Meadows toward Thunder Mountain Pass and the Thunder Mountain Lakes basin, then approaching the peak's north side. The standard SE-slope scramble route is reached via Upper Thunder Mountain Lake.

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Thunder Mountain Lakes
bivy.notes: Lake basin under the granite of Slippery Slab Tower and Thunder Mountain, reached by the unofficial trail south from Trap Pass. The closest camp to the north face. Fragile ground; camp only on rock or bare sites.
bivy.water: The lakes
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few small sites on durable ground

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. No campfires above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

peak: Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower

name: Northwest Ridge
approach: Start at the Mirror Lake trailhead at the end of Forest Road 5480, a short drive from I-90 exit 62, at about 3,600 ft. Hike the Mirror Lake trail about 1 mile to the Cottonwood Lake spur, then roughly 0.6 mile more to the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn north on the PCT for about 0.6 mile to the point where a boot path leaves the trail on the left and climbs toward the peak's northwest ridge.

name: Southeast Spur (East Peak)
approach: Start at the Mirror Lake trailhead at the end of Forest Road 5480 (about 3,600 ft). Hike the Mirror Lake trail to the lake, mostly level, then follow the PCT to the lake's south end and find the boot path.

name: North Couloir
approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road, ~23.1 mi from Marblemount), travel via Cascade Pass or the nearby Alliteration Col and descend/traverse east through the Pelton Basin area to Trapper Lake (el. ~4,170 ft), sitting just northeast of Trapper Mountain. From the lake, boot or skin directly to the base of the obvious north-facing couloir splitting the summit block, switching to crampons/ski (ascent) plates as the snow firms up higher on the route.
descent: Ski, splitboard, or downclimb the same couloir back to Trapper Lake, then climb back out via Cascade Pass/Alliteration Col to the trailhead.

bivy.name: Trapper Lake
bivy.notes: Glacial lake directly below the north couloir. Reached from the Cascade Pass side over Alliteration Col, or by a steep, poorly marked path up from the upper Stehekin River trail. The slopes above it slide often in spring.
bivy.water: Lake water, treat it
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few informal tent sites near the shore; cross-country camping, no established site

bivy.name: Pelton Basin Camp
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin sits about half a mile east of and below Cascade Pass, on the Stehekin side, which makes it the obvious first night for a party coming in over the pass rather than up from the lake. It puts Horseshoe Basin within a long day, though the basin itself is still several miles and a substantial descent-then-climb away. Snow lingers here well into summer and the trail across the basin can be hard to follow when it does, so early-season parties should expect to navigate rather than follow tread.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creek through the basin, though flow drops late in a dry summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp on the Recreation.gov system, and among the harder Cascade Pass sites to draw in midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp — the number of sites is not published, and it is few enough that it goes early on summer weekends. Assume it may be full and carry a plan that does not depend on it.

name: Up In Arms
approach: Follow the Blue Lake Trail toward the Beckey Gully; just as you reach Concord Tower's west face, head uphill staying close to the wall to the base of the route, well to climber's left of the South Face routes.
descent: Two rappels on a single 60 m rope down to the notch between Concord and Lexington towers, then walk off down the gully (approach shoes recommended).

name: Upper North Ridge w/Great Gendarme
approach: From I-90 Exit 85, take Highway 970 east 7 miles to Teanaway Road, then bear right onto North Fork Teanaway Road continuing 22.5 miles total. From trailhead: via Lake Ingalls and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass, then east across the Stuart Glacier to the North Ridge notch
descent: Cascadian Couloir

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Lake Trailhead (North Fork Teanaway Rd, FR 9737)

name: Standard Route (Headlee Pass)
approach: From the Sunrise Mine trailhead, Trail 707 crosses several streams in the first mile, including the main South Fork Stillaguamish, which has no bridge and can be a serious obstacle when runoff is high. The trail then climbs through forest and an open talus basin before tightening into steep, narrow switchbacks up the couloir to Headlee Pass, about 2.7 miles from the trailhead. From the pass, the trail traverses the south flank of Sperry Peak into the upper Vesper Creek basin, where the route leaves the lake trail at the creek crossing.

name: West Face
approach: The genuine standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of South Peak's granite faces; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

name: West Slope - East Arete (Original Route)
approach: Same general Southern Pickets approach as the South Route — via Goodell Creek, The Barrier, and Crescent Creek Basin — continuing to the notch/saddle between Himmelhorn and West Twin Needle rather than climbing directly from the basin.
descent: Downclimb the class 2 west slope back to the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the separate Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is legally awkward: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is not on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is walk-up only — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

name: Western Dihedral
approach: South Face is the southwest-facing slab wall around the corner west of the Illusion Wall, with its own approach separate from Waterfall Basin. Take I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing to the brown Squire Creek Trail #654 sign and 8-10 minutes beyond it, to two cut logs either side of the road with old logging cable visible. Turn right a few steps past them on a well-beaten boot track, drop to Squire Creek and ford it where it is shallowest (hard in early season or after storms), then follow the climbers' track briefly downstream before it turns uphill, crosses a tributary and climbs old-growth forest and two gullies, steep and dirty near the top, to the grassy saddle, about 3 hours from the car. For this route go left (west) from the saddle to the base of Skeena26, scramble about 100 m of class 4 ramps and small dihedrals to a large shelf, follow it left to a deep gully (two-bolt anchor for a hand line or a short rappel), cross it and follow a cairned boot track west across talus and cedar ribs to the large talus field below the far western wall, about an hour from Skeena26.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a county park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A moving target and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
bivy.permit: None
bivy.capacity: Small ledges, one party

waypoints.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
Top of Western Dihedral (far western wall)

name: North Ridge
approach: Park on the wide paved shoulder of SR-20 about three quarters of a mile west of the signed Blue Lake trailhead lot, on the north side, where there is no guard rail. A good climbers' trail leads from the road through forest into the basin. No pass is needed at the pullout; the Blue Lake lot needs a forest pass.

name: Windy Peak via Iron Gate Trailhead (Boundary Trail / Sunny Pass Approach)
approach: From Loomis, take County Road #9425 north 2 miles to County Road #4066/FR-39; follow FR-39 about 14 miles, then turn onto FR-3900-500 and follow it about 6 miles (high-clearance vehicle recommended, not advised for passenger cars) to the Iron Gate Trailhead. Hike north on the Boundary Trail toward Sunny Pass.
descent: Reverse via Sunny Pass and the Boundary Trail back to the Iron Gate Trailhead.

bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Windy Peak and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. Expect burn. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a free self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.
